packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person study spanning five European countries, defaults produced medium-to-large effects on risk-taking, but also lowered ratings of the advisor's advice, especially when the targeted default was refused — with framing of the default question shifting outcomes by smaller amounts.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, on financial risk-taking decisions with wealth-manager defaults.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly answers the EU dark-pattern question in the brief: defaults move behavior but can damage perceived trustworthiness of the institution, especially when a poorly-fitted default is refused — a real reputational-risk signal for choosing opt-out enrollment or a mismatched preset multiplier.
limitations: single-session experimental measure, no 6-12 month persistence data
wealth-management risk allocation rather than round-up savings specifically
packets.relevance_reason: EU-based, consumer self-directed financial-decision evidence on when a default reads as helpful versus manipulative, directly informing the reputational-risk constraint in the brief.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce debt, partly because it also reduced autopay enrollment and increased missed payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on real credit-card accounts with six-month follow-up.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's central worry: a choice-architecture change can move the enrollment/behavior number without moving the outcome that matters, and can create new harm (missed payments) for liquidity-constrained users — the clearest self-directed consumer-financial analogue we have.
limitations: credit-card debt repayment, not a savings feature
shrouding a default is a stronger intervention than the opt-in/opt-out/active-choice menu under consideration
packets.relevance_reason: Shows a default/nudge changing nominal enrollment behavior while failing to change the substantive financial outcome, in a genuinely consumer self-directed financial product.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once job turnover, balance withdrawal at separation, and opt-out from escalation are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalated employees escalate on the first date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation and withdrawal dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrollment gains are much smaller in steady state than the headline participation-rate effect suggests.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-plan turnover dynamics (vesting, job separation) don't map onto a banking app
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults durably raise saving amounts, using the most rigorous long-run design available.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller and less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across campaign websites' default rollout timing, 2020 US election.
packets.why_it_matters: A rare study of a recurring-financial-commitment default in a self-directed consumer setting, showing such defaults disproportionately affect naive and small users and generate regret (refunds) — directly relevant to the dark-pattern and vulnerable-user risk of defaulting people into ongoing round-up saving.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings or banking product
US setting rather than EU consumer-protection regulatory context
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the simple defaults-always-help premise by documenting donor regret/refunds and disproportionate impact on inexperienced, small contributors from a recurring financial default.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Structural analysis of 8.6 million tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence comes from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together; adding a lower option to a fixed default menu (a 15% tip below 20/25/30%) captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data, validated against an independent stated-preference survey.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a transferable method and finding for the level-preset decision: a menu of preset multipliers with one selected functions like the tip-menu structure studied here, and shows how adding/adjusting the menu of preset options shifts welfare and adherence — directly informs whether to add a lower multiplier option and where to anchor it.
limitations: taxi tipping, not a savings product
consumer preferences for tipping norms may not generalize to savings-rate preferences
packets.relevance_reason: Provides a directly transferable structural-model method for reasoning about preset-menu design (which default to pick, what happens if you add another option) — the mechanism explicitly named as analogous to the round-up multiplier decision.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
packets.methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework-building across the consumer-defaults literature. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the team a structured way to predict and measure whether the round-up default's effect on enrollment will persist or decay by 6-12 months, and what moderators (salience, prior intent) to watch for.
limitations: theoretical/synthesis paper, no new effect-size estimates
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: General consumer-behavior review addressing exactly the persistence-of-defaults question the brief asks about, in a non-employer setting.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Automatic (opt-out) enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts at UK banks reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in market-wide annual savings, though alerts captured less than half of consumers' potential savings.
packets.methodology: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks.
packets.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that opt-out default enrollment into a protective banking feature produces large, real, at-scale behavioral effects in the same UK consumer-banking context as our app, directly supporting opt-out as a viable entry design.
limitations: Feature is a warning alert rather than a savings-contribution decision with a preset level
Does not report 6-12 month persistence, withdrawal, or complaint outcomes
packets.relevance_reason: Closest real-world consumer-banking analogue to opt-out enrollment into a beneficial feature, quantifying the scale of the default effect.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: In an RCT of behavioral nudges for voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, with heterogeneous backfire effects by income, education, and gender.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey, n=220.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that defaults reliably raise participation, showing default-option nudges can backfire and reduce contribution willingness for specific demographic segments — a strong caution before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: Voluntary pension saving survey in China, cultural/institutional context differs from EU consumer banking
Small sample (n=220) and stated intent rather than observed behavior
packets.relevance_reason: One of the few studies here finding default options backfire rather than help, directly answering the brief's request for evidence contradicting the defaults-always-help premise.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: This overview of behavioral household finance synthesizes evidence on consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, and asset allocation, and reviews interventions including choice architecture and product design that firms and governments use to shape household financial behavior.
packets.methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter (NBER), abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest available synthesis on consumer (not employer-mediated) financial choice architecture, giving a framework for weighing defaults, active choice, and product design against the brief's two open decisions.
limitations: a narrative synthesis, not a quantitative meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
abstract does not specify household-finance-specific default effect magnitudes
packets.relevance_reason: The review-type synthesis the brief asks for, in the consumer/household finance setting closest to the product being built.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: Payment reminders reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while other users saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, studying direct and indirect effects of nudging on fee outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern about who is helped and who is hurt: a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer fintech setting produced a subgroup that was made worse off, which is exactly the distributional risk the round-up enrolment decision needs to guard against before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
Brazilian credit/overdraft context rather than EU round-up savings
no measurement of persistence at 6-12 months, only aggregate fee outcomes
no active-choice comparison arm
packets.relevance_reason: Strong evidence on heterogeneous/distributional effects of a financial nudge and a clear contradiction of the 'nudges/defaults always help' premise, in a self-directed consumer financial app setting.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision with no default) and an 'enhanced active choice' variant (highlighting losses from the non-preferred option) can motivate behavior change, including savings behavior, as an alternative or complement to automatic enrollment.
alternates.methodology: Literature review plus a series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice designs.
alternates.why_it_matters: This is the paper that directly tests the third enrolment option the brief is deciding between — active choice — and proposes a concrete enhanced variant, giving a design alternative to opt-out that avoids the ethical/manipulation concerns of automatic enrollment.
limitations: field experiments span health (medication adherence) and savings domains, not specifically a consumer fintech app
abstract does not report enrolment or persistence effect sizes
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly addresses C6, the active-choice-vs-default comparison at the heart of the entry-design decision.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual from 15 months post-rollout onward, with differences tied to rollout scope.
alternates.methodology: Difference-in-differences analysis around the EU DMA choice-screen rollout on iOS and Android.
alternates.why_it_matters: Direct, large-scale, real-world evidence that mandatory active choice screens in mobile apps under EU regulation substantially shift outcomes away from incumbent defaults, strong evidence for how much benefit active choice could capture versus opt-out.
limitations: Browser choice, not a financial-savings decision
Does not measure engagement or persistence of the choice made, only usage share
alternates.relevance_reason: The clearest EU regulatory precedent quantifying forced active choice against incumbent defaults in a mobile-app context, central to the entry-design decision.
alternates.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
alternates.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
alternates.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

alternates.key_finding: Across 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios with 2,100 Australians, people rate interventions positively overall, strongly prefer System-2 (reflective) framings and saving-framed messages, and transparency has no significant effect on approval or perceived manipulation.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered vignette survey experiment, representative Australian sample, 2x2x2-style manipulation of transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly informs how to frame the round-up default and multiplier copy to avoid a dark-pattern read: saving-framed, System-2-style prompts are best received, and disclosure of mechanism does not hurt approval, which de-risks an opt-out design if messaged this way.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios, not a live product with real money at stake
measures stated approval, not actual enrollment or savings behaviour
alternates.relevance_reason: Speaks directly to the EU dark-pattern/manipulation-perception risk named in the brief for choosing between opt-out framings.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns and proposes a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable defaults from manipulative choice architecture.
alternates.methodology: Legal/doctrinal analysis and taxonomy development; abstract-only.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU-law framework for judging whether an opt-out or pre-selected default counts as an autonomy-violating dark pattern, directly informing the entry-design decision's reputational/legal risk.
limitations: Legal/normative analysis, no empirical effect-size data
Not specific to financial products or savings apps
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern risk the brief flags as a reputational concern for defaulting users into the feature.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default is a poor fit, with active-choice variation driven by transitory shocks rather than attentiveness.
alternates.methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative dataset.
alternates.why_it_matters: Strong evidence that defaults can persist regardless of value-mismatch and that heterogeneity in 'who opts out' is largely random rather than driven by informed choice — a caution against assuming active choosers are the engaged ones.
limitations: health-insurance enrollment, not a consumer financial product
low-income Medicare population differs from a mobile banking app's user base
alternates.relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and insensitivity to option value, directly bearing on distributional/manipulation-risk questions even though the setting differs.
alternates.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
alternates.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.
